texts.text: Abstract

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Recent advances in photorealistic avatar generation have enabled highly realistic talking-head avatars, raising security concerns regarding identity impersonation in AI-mediated communication. To advance in this challenging problem, the task of avatar fingerprinting aims to determine whether two avatar videos are driven by the same human operator or not. However, current public databases in the literature are scarce and based solely on old-fashioned talking-head avatar generators, not representing realistic scenarios for the current task of avatar fingerprinting. To overcome this situation, the present article introduces AVAPrintDB, a new publicly available multi-generator talking-head avatar database for avatar fingerprinting. AVAPrintDB is constructed from two audiovisual corpora and three stateof-the-art avatar generators (GAGAvatar, LivePortrait, HunyuanPortrait), representing different synthesis paradigms, and includes both self- and crossreenactments to simulate legitimate usage and impersonation scenarios.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Recent progress in photorealistic avatar generation has enabled the synthesis of highly realistic talking-head avatars from a single picture, significantly advancing applications in telepresence [1], virtual reality [2], digital humans [3], and AI-mediated communication [4]. Large technology companies 1 and startups 2 are actively investing in avatar-based interfaces, with applications ranging from virtual assistants and customer service agents to remote collaboration platforms and personalized digital identities [4]. Industry reports 3 estimate that the global market for digital humans and avatar-based communication systems is expected to grow rapidly in the coming years, driven by advances in generative AI and increasing adoption of immersive communication technologies.

texts.orig: At the same time, the widespread availability of realistic avatar generation tools introduces new security and privacy risks. Recent incidents have demonstrated that synthetic media can be exploited for impersonation attacks, social engineering, and identity fraud. For instance, DeepFake-based scams 4 have been used to impersonate executives in video calls and fraudulently authorize financial transactions, leading to losses of millions of dollars in real-world cases 5 . As avatar-based communication becomes more prevalent, these risks extend beyond static DeepFakes to interactive, real-time impersonation scenarios, where an attacker can control a synthetic avatar that visually appears to be a legitimate user.

texts.orig: In such settings, traditional authentication methods based on appearance (e.g., biometric face recognition [5, 6]) become unreliable, since the avatar's visual identity is fully synthetic and can be arbitrarily chosen or manipulated. This shift fundamentally changes the authentication problem: instead of verifying who the avatar looks like, the system must determine who is controlling the avatar. This task is known in the literature as avatar fingerprinting [7]. Formally, the goal of avatar fingerprinting is to determine whether two avatar videos are driven by the same underlying human identity. Given two synthetic avatar videos V1 and V2, generated by potentially different avatar synthesis pipelines, the system must determine whether the underlying driver identities match. It is important to highlight that the task of avatar fingerprinting differs from the task of DeepFakes detection [8, 9, 10], where the main goal is to distinguish real from synthetic content. In avatar fingerprint both samples are synthetic.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Avatar fingerprinting addresses the problem of determining whether a synthetic avatar video is driven by its legitimate user or not, focusing on identity cues preserved in facial motion dynamics rather than visual appearance alone. The problem is also related to behavioral biometrics [27, 28], where identity is inferred from human dynamic patterns such as gait, keystroke, or facial motion. Unlike traditional face recognition, which relies heavily on appearance cues, avatar fingerprinting must operate under conditions where appearance is synthetically generated and therefore unreliable.

texts.text: 2.1. Photorealistic Talking-Head Avatar Generation

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Photorealistic talking-head avatar generation aims to animate a target identity using the facial motion and head pose extracted from a driving signal, typically a video sequence. This task is also commonly referred to as portrait animation [29], motion transfer [30], or talking-head reenactment [31]. It is important to remark that this task differs from related problems such as novel-view synthesis [32], full 3D head reconstruction [33], or audio-driven animation [34], as the goal is to preserve the appearance of a reference identity while faithfully transferring motion dynamics from another source.
texts.text: Photorealistic talking-head avatar generation aims to animate a target identity using the facial motion and head pose extracted from a driving signal, typically a video sequence. This task is also commonly referred to as portrait animation [29], motion transfer [30], or talking-head reenactment [31]. It is important to remark that this task differs from related problems such as novel-view synthesis [32], full 3D head reconstruction [33], or audio-driven animation [34], as the goal is to preserve the appearance of a reference identity while faithfully transferring motion dynamics from another source.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Early approaches to facial reenactment relied on parametric face models and 3D morphable models to retarget expressions and head pose, enabling real-time portrait manipulation and reenactment [35, 36]. The emergence of deep generative models enabled realistic reenactment from minimal input, particularly through motion transfer methods that animate a single portrait using learned keypoint dynamics [13, 37]. Subsequent advances in neural rendering and implicit scene representations improved realism and view consistency [38, 39], while recent diffusion-based video generation techniques have further increased photorealism and temporal coherence [24, 40].

texts.label: text
texts.orig: To date, the number of public databases and benchmarks specifically designed for avatar fingerprinting is very limited. The NVFAIR database introduced by NVIDIA [7] is currently the largest collection of reenacted talkinghead videos, with more than 600,000 videos. NVFAIR comprises scripted and free-form monologues from 46 captured subjects (real data) as well as synthetic reenactments generated with three methods (FaceVid2Vid [13], TPS [14], and LIA [15]), although they are considered old-fashioned nowadays in comparison to state-of-the-art avatar generators, as discussed in Sec. 2.1. In total NVFAIR covers 161 unique identities (by including additional CREMA-D [20] and RAVDESS [21] speakers) with self- and crossreenactments. Access to NVFAIR is restricted via a request form. Also, benchmarking is not possible as the proposed avatar fingerprinting system is not publicly available.

texts.text: 2.3. Avatar Fingerprinting Systems

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The task of avatar fingerprinting is formulated as a pairwise decision problem: given two avatar videos, the goal is to determine whether they are driven by the same underlying identity or not. This differs from authentication, which evaluates a sample against a claimed identity (e.g., access control scenarios), and from identification, where a sample is matched against a gallery of known identities. Avatar fingerprinting constitutes the most fundamental setting, as it isolates the ability of a model to capture identity-dependent behavioral signals without relying on predefined identity classes.

texts.orig: Early works on avatar fingerprinting demonstrated that such behavioral cues persist through avatar generation. In [7], identity was modeled through facial landmark dynamics using temporal convolutional networks, showing that user-specific motion patterns can be discriminative even in highly realistic avatars (they achieved around 87% AUC in their best setting). Similarly, [11, 12] proposed a graph-based approach that captures structured relationships between facial landmarks over time, obtaining similar results in their respective experiments (86.6% and 83% AUC respectively).

texts.orig: We select two widely used video datasets in the literature as they consider realistic scenarios for avatar fingerprinting: CREMA-D [20] and RAVDESS [21]. Our selection is guided by three main considerations. First, both datasets are distributed under permissive licenses that allow redistribution and derivative use, making them suitable for constructing and releasing a reproducible benchmark. Second, they have been employed in prior work on avatar fingerprinting and behavioral biometric analysis, including [7, 12, 45], which facilitates continuity. Third, they include structured variations in emotional expression and scripted utterances. These characteristics enable controlled experimental protocols in which different subjects can be evaluated while producing identical sentences and emotional expressions. Such control is essential for avatar fingerprinting studies, as it allows identity-related motion cues to be isolated from linguistic content, affective expression, and other confounding factors. For example, the datasets make it possible to compare avatars of different individuals speaking the same sentence with similar affect, or the same individual rendered through different avatar pipelines, enabling fine-grained evaluation of biometric consistency.

texts.text: 3.2. Photorealistic Talking-Head Avatar Generators

texts.label: text
texts.orig: A key aspect of our proposed AVAPrintDB is the inclusion of multiple state-of-the-art avatar generators, each relying on different modeling assumptions and motion transfer mechanisms: one from the Gaussian splatting family (GAGAvatar [22]), one from the warping-based family (LivePortrait [23]), and one from the diffusion-based family (HunyuanPortrait [24]). These three generators are selected as they represent distinct synthesis paradigms and therefore introduce different types of motion transfer artifacts that may influence the avatar fingerprinting task. They are specifically selected due to practical considerations of availability, efficiency, and quality. GAGAvatar [22] is a one-shot 3D Gaussian head avatar method that reconstructs a controllable 3D head from a single image in a single forward pass. It is lightweight in GPU memory and offers real-time reenactment speeds thanks to its efficient 3D Gaussian representation, making it easy to use for our purposes. LivePortrait [23] provides a fast, efficient 2D animation solution with minimal memory overhead, and the code/models are publicly available. LivePortrait's ease of use and high speed, combined with qualitatively good visual results, made it a practical choice for our comparisons. Finally, HunyuanPortrait [24] considers a state-of-the-art diffusion model. Although diffusion models are heavier, HunyuanPortrait is open-source and produces great visual fidelity and temporal consistency. Its inclusion allows to evaluate a high-quality diffusion approach against the faster lightweight methods.

texts.orig: From a biometric behavioral perspective, the generation process can be interpreted as a transformation that maps real facial motion into a synthetic domain. Ideally, this transformation should preserve identity-specific temporal patterns while altering appearance. However, in practice, avatar generators may introduce biases, artifacts, or normalization effects that partially suppress or modify these cues. As a result, models trained or evaluated on a single generator may inadvertently learn generator-specific artifacts instead of robust behavioral patterns. To address this limitation, our proposed benchmark incorporates multiple generators with diverse characteristics, enabling systematic evaluation under intra- and cross-generator conditions. This design allows us to analyze whether avatar fingerprinting systems generalize across synthesis pipelines or rely on artifacts tied to a specific generator.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Based on the the curated datasets described in Sec. 3.1 and the avatar generators described in Sec. 3.2, we construct our proposed AVAPrintDB designed to support controlled and reproducible evaluation of avatar fingerprinting systems. Each generated video is defined by a target identity (which determines the avatar appearance) and a driving identity (which provides the motion dynamics). This setup enables both self-reenactment (same target and driver) and cross-reenactment (different target and driver), as shown in Fig. 1, which are essential for evaluating avatar fingerprinting. Every targetdriver pair is rendered with the same three avatar generators, ensuring that each underlying motion instance is available under three different synthesis conditions. Additionally, all avatar videos are generated using a consistent protocol. For the target images, we manually select a single frontal, neutralexpression frame per subject from the curated dataset. Manual selection ensures that the chosen frames are free of occlusions, head rotations, or strong expressions that could introduce artifacts during reenactment. Fig. 1 shows visual examples of avatars generated using the three selected methods, illustrating the process of generating self-reenactments and cross-reenactments across different time frames in the video. We describe next the specific details to build the self- and cross-reenactment pairs of our proposed AVAPrintDB.

We hypothesize that some generators may preserve behavioral cues in a way that transfers better across synthesis pipelines, whereas others may induce representations that are more generator-specific. texts.orig: The fairness analysis is conducted at the level of verification trials. Each trial consists of an enrollment video V e and a test video V t , where the enrollment sample always corresponds to a self-reenactment (genuine avatar), while the test sample may be either genuine or impostor. To assess demographic effects in a consistent manner, we define all subgroup labels (gender, ethnicity, and age) based exclusively on the enrollment identity, i.e., the identity associated with V e . This design choice reflects the intended application scenario of avatar-based authentication, where the system verifies whether a query sample matches a claimed identity. In particular, the enrollment identity represents the individual who may be subject to impersonation, and therefore constitutes the reference point for analyzing fairness.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This article introduces AVAPrintDB, a publicly available multi-generator photorealistic talking-head avatar database and benchmark for the task of avatar fingerprinting. Its main strength is that it enables, for the first time in a fully reproducible way, controlled evaluation of avatar fingerprinting systems across multiple state-of-the-art synthesis pipelines and source datasets. This makes it possible to study whether current avatar fingerprinting systems truly capture identity-related behavioral cues or instead rely on generatoror dataset-specific artifacts.
texts.text: This article introduces AVAPrintDB, a publicly available multi-generator photorealistic talking-head avatar database and benchmark for the task of avatar fingerprinting. Its main strength is that it enables, for the first time in a fully reproducible way, controlled evaluation of avatar fingerprinting systems across multiple state-of-the-art synthesis pipelines and source datasets. This makes it possible to study whether current avatar fingerprinting systems truly capture identity-related behavioral cues or instead rely on generatoror dataset-specific artifacts.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The proposed benchmark and results achieved using two state-of-theart public avatar fingerprinting systems highlight two main findings. First, avatar fingerprinting is feasible under controlled conditions, supporting the hypothesis that identity-related motion cues can persist after avatar synthesis. Second, current avatar fingerprinting systems remain sensitive to both generator and dataset shift. These results indicate that present methods do not yet learn fully robust and invariant behavioral representations.

We hope it facilitates the development of more robust and practically useful avatar fingerprinting systems for authentication in avatar-mediated communication.
